title: His family carried the dead cattle
hook: Ravidas sings that his family carried dead animals near Benares, yet great men bow to him now (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)

segments.voice: Yesterday, gareeb nivaaj: the one who cherishes the poor, holding a king's canopy over a leather-worker's head. Today, Ravidas names his family's trade out loud.

Before dawn, a truck stops outside, and someone you'll never meet carries off your trash. A worker in a hospital basement washes what nobody wants to wash. Somewhere, a person handles the dead so the rest of us don't have to. These jobs get noticed mostly by their absence, the day they aren't done. In Raag Malar, Ravidas opens a hymn by addressing the whole town and naming his family's work. Not hinting at it. Naming it.
screen: `THE TRUCK BEFORE DAWN.` → `JOBS WE KNOW BY THEIR ABSENCE.` → `RAVIDAS NAMES HIS FAMILY'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Two hymns sit side by side on Ang 1293 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Four days ago this path heard the second, with the learned bowing. Today, start with the first. It opens, in paraphrase: people of the town, my caste is well known; it is the leather-workers' caste. And in my heart I hold the Lord's virtues. Then a picture from a scribe's desk. The palm tree is counted impure, and so is the paper made from its leaves. But when the Lord's praise is written on that paper, people bow before it and worship it. The material doesn't change. What's written on it changes how it's treated. Ravidas sets himself right there: the same family, the same trade, and the Name written into him. The second hymn adds one small word that carries a lot: still. His relatives, he says, still go around Benares hauling away dead cattle. He doesn't say they used to, or that he got out, so the honor can't be explained by escape. Brahmins of careful conduct bow before him anyway, and he calls himself the servant of the Lord's servants. In that same hymn he names Kabir too, as if to say: the Lord keeps doing this. He doesn't ask to be reclassified, or call the work beneath him. Sikh teaching has a name for honest work: kirat karni, earning by your own labor. So today's line, every job is holy, isn't Ravidas's exact phrase. It's what his song does: it names a job the town shrank from, right at the top, and doesn't apologize.
screen: `PEOPLE OF THE TOWN, MY CASTE IS KNOWN.` · `PALM-LEAF PAPER, BOWED TO WHEN IT HOLDS PRAISE.` · `STILL HAULING DEAD CATTLE IN BENARES.` · then, large: `NO APOLOGY FOR THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Trace something you touched today back to the hands that dealt with its mess: the drain, the bin, the floor, the laundry, the shoes. Let one of those workers come to mind, even without a face, and stay with them a few breaths, without pity, the way Ravidas stays with his family's work. Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.
Kirat karni. Sikh teaching's name for earning by your own labor: Ravidas naming his family's trade before the whole town, and not apologizing for it.
Your line: every job is holy. Someone's hard work is holding up your day. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear these hymns of Ravidas in the gurdwara as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Sikh ideal of kirat karni, honest work, honors labor of every kind.

chat.says: Did Ravidas hide his family's work once he became a famous saint?
options: No. He named their trade to the whole town, and said they still haul dead cattle.
Yes. He said his family had left that work behind once he found the Lord.
Partly. He named it, but asked to be counted in a higher caste now.
chat.meaning: In his Malar hymns Ravidas names his caste to the whole town and says his relatives still haul dead cattle, yet Brahmins bow to him.

kirat karni.meaning: earning by your own honest labor

Malar.meaning: the raag, or musical mode, of these hymns

notes: Both Malar hymns paraphrased from memory; please confirm both are on Ang 1293 and that 'jaa kai kutamb' is the hymn that also names Namdev and Kabir.
